archive.title: Extinction and biodiversity
archive.body: Extinction is the permanent disappearance of a species, while the loss of local populations can occur long before global extinction. Human pressures include habitat conversion, overexploitation, invasive organisms, pollution and climate change. The relationship between genetic diversity, population resilience and conservation intervention provides the context for evaluating de-extinction. [1,11]

archive.title: Ancient DNA and authentication
archive.body: Ancient DNA can survive in bones, teeth and preserved tissue but is often short, chemically damaged and mixed with environmental or modern DNA. Authenticity requires careful sampling, contamination controls, characteristic fragment and damage patterns, and comparison across independent evidence. Recovered sequence fragments are molecular information, not viable cells. [9,10]

archive.title: Sequencing and comparative genomics
archive.body: Sequencing produces reads that must be quality controlled and assembled or aligned against reference genomes. Reference-guided reconstruction can miss divergent regions and may bias inferred sequence toward a living relative. Comparative genomics identifies conserved sequences and candidate variants, but sequence association alone does not establish the cause of a trait. The Christmas Island rat analysis illustrates reconstruction limits. [10]

archive.title: Genome editing and reproduction
archive.body: CRISPR-guided editing changes selected genomic sites in living cells; multiplexing can target several sites but requires validation of intended edits and unintended changes. SCNT is relevant to some mammalian cloning strategies. Avian primordial germ cells offer a distinct route to inherited changes in birds, although engineering germ cells does not itself establish viable dodo production. [2,7,8]

archive.title: Species evidence archive
archive.body: Each species profile includes history and extinction drivers; available ancient or historical material; nearest useful living relatives; peer-reviewed genomic achievements; programme announcements; reproductive obstacles; ecological questions; and an evidence-labelled conclusion. See Section E for complete editorial text.

archive.title: Case-study library
archive.body: Pyrenean ibex: short-lived cloned offspring, demonstrating developmental barriers [2]. Quagga and aurochs: phenotype-oriented back-breeding, not exact genetic recovery [12]. Christmas Island rat: genome reconstruction limitations [10]. Black-footed ferret: conservation cloning and breeding [13]. Kākāpō: species-wide genomics for management [14]. Ancient Silene: regeneration from preserved plant tissue, not revival of an extinct species [15].

archive.title: Ethics, ecology and feasibility
archive.body: Evaluate genomic completeness, viable reproduction, population genetic diversity, suitable habitat, disease risk, animal welfare, ecological interactions, conservation priorities and long-term funding. Modelling suggests de-extinction spending can create opportunity costs when it displaces protection of living threatened species. [11,16]

species.name: Woolly mammoth
species.body: The woolly mammoth inhabited northern Pleistocene environments. Ancient specimens from cold settings have yielded DNA and, in an exceptional 52,000-year-old skin sample, preserved chromosome-scale spatial organisation. The 2024 Cell study assembled 28 chromosome-length scaffolds using PaleoHi-C. This improves understanding of ancient genome architecture but does not provide a living mammoth cell. Contemporary proposals examine mammoth-associated adaptations in elephant-derived cells. Key obstacles include identifying causal variants for complex traits, validating edits, achieving viable reproduction, animal welfare, and demonstrating that a proxy would have an appropriate ecological role. Status: peer-reviewed genomic research; proposed reproductive restoration. [9,11]

species.name: Dodo
species.body: The dodo was a flightless bird endemic to Mauritius that disappeared after human arrival and associated ecological disruption. Historical specimens enable investigation of its evolutionary history. The Nicobar pigeon is a close living relative and a valuable genomic comparison: a 2025 peer-reviewed study reported a chromosome-level Nicobar pigeon assembly. In 2025 Colossal announced progress culturing pigeon primordial germ cells and engineering avian surrogate systems; these are programme-reported milestones, not evidence that a living dodo has been produced. Remaining obstacles include reconstructing relevant variants, avian germline transmission, viable development and habitat restoration. [7,8,11]

species.name: Thylacine
species.body: The thylacine was a marsupial carnivore whose last known captive individual died in 1936. A peer-reviewed 2022 study produced a chromosome-scale hybrid genome assembly from historical material. A University of Melbourne announcement in 2024 described a newer reconstruction estimated at more than 99.9% accuracy and progress editing dunnart cells; this percentage must be attributed to the team rather than presented as independently established complete recovery. The fat-tailed dunnart is a research model and living relative, not a straightforward surrogate for an adult thylacine. Challenges include genome function, marsupial reproduction, embryonic development and ecological suitability. [5,6]

species.name: Dire wolf
species.body: The dire wolf was a deeply divergent extinct canid lineage. In 2025 Colossal announced three grey-wolf-derived animals engineered to display selected dire-wolf-like features. Published commentary describes 20 edits at 14 genomic loci and argues that these are engineered proxies rather than restored dire wolves. The company’s announcement is a technological claim; the independent scientific debate concerns the extent of genetic difference, phenotype, species identity and conservation purpose. This case provides a strong demonstration that recreating visible characteristics is not equivalent to restoring a historical genome or ecosystem. [3,4]

intro.title: The biodiversity crisis
intro.body: Biodiversity describes variation among living organisms, including genetic diversity within species, diversity among species, and the ecosystems they form. Its decline affects ecological processes such as pollination, seed dispersal, nutrient cycling, grazing and predation. The 2026 Living Planet Report estimates that the average size of monitored vertebrate wildlife populations declined by 73% from 1970 to 2022. This indicator measures relative population trends in the monitored dataset; it is not a count of animals lost or a measure of the percentage of species that have become extinct. [1]

intro.title: What is de-extinction?
intro.body: De-extinction encompasses scientific efforts to recreate organisms resembling extinct species, recover selected genetic or physical characteristics, or develop ecological proxies intended to perform functions formerly associated with lost organisms. The term is debated because a living organism with some extinct traits is not necessarily genetically, developmentally or ecologically identical to the historical species. The IUCN recommends evaluating proxies according to potential conservation benefits and risks rather than treating physical resemblance as proof of species restoration. [11]

intro.title: Three approaches
intro.body: Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) places a donor somatic-cell nucleus into an egg whose nucleus has been removed. This has produced cloned mammals and, in the case of the extinct Pyrenean ibex subspecies, a short-lived newborn. Genome editing instead alters selected DNA sequences in cells from a living relative; it may generate animals displaying extinct-like traits but does not reconstruct all genomic and developmental differences. Selective back-breeding uses existing variation in living populations to favour characteristics resembling an extinct form, as seen in quagga-like zebras and aurochs-like cattle. Each approach differs in its biological requirements, limitations and definition of success. [2,3,11,12]

intro.title: Website mission
intro.body: DE-EXTINCTION LAB is an interactive evidence-based science exhibition that investigates what genomics can reveal about extinct species, which technologies have been demonstrated, and which scientific or ecological challenges remain unresolved. Visitors can explore through a narrative expedition or examine the detailed research archives. Both routes lead to the same principle: recovering ancient DNA, creating a modified cell, producing a viable organism and restoring a sustainable species are distinct milestones.

cases: • Pyrenean ibex (bucardo): SCNT produced a live-born animal after extinction of the subspecies, but it died shortly afterward with lung abnormalities. This illustrates the difference between a birth and sustainable recovery [3].
• Quagga: selective breeding of plains zebras for quagga-like striping is a phenotype-focused proxy effort, not restoration of the historical quagga genome [2].
• Aurochs: cattle back-breeding projects seek ancestral-looking or ecological traits; these are not genetically identical aurochs [2].
• Christmas Island rat: ancient genome reconstruction can omit functionally relevant genomic regions when reference genomes diverge [4].

• Black-footed ferret: conservation cloning using cryopreserved cells demonstrates the application of reproductive biotechnology to an endangered living species. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Smithsonian provide institutional updates [8].
• Kākāpō: species-wide genomic sequencing has provided information useful for conservation management and breeding decisions [9].
• Silene stenophylla: regeneration of fertile plants from ancient preserved tissue demonstrates unusual plant-tissue viability; the species itself is not extinct, so this is not de-extinction [10].
